t65z13_st1p3w1p1: Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: "Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, give you ideas, or some mix?" Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time. If it's obvious what they want, go with that. If it isn't, that one sentence can keep you from advising somebody who's thinking, "I just need you to hear this." Or from just listening while they're asking for help thinking.
t65z13_st1p6w1p1: Community can work in two directions. Sometimes loving people make you feel safe enough, and like you belong, that a deeper opening can happen. Other times the opening comes first and changes the kinds of people and relationships you can "manifest." You might wonder where all these loving people came from. Then community helps you make the opening practical and real, and live it in your body. The loop matters more than which door you came in through: love moves from spiritual experience to your little one, from your little one into the grown-up relationship, from you into other people, and back again.
t65z13_st1p4w1p1: The three grown-up jobs work between people too. A good peer (someone you take turns listening to, as equals) can lend you the Nurturer by being warm company. And the Protector, by keeping what you say private and sticking to the time you agreed on. If you say no, they don't push. But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places.
t65z13_st1p2w2p1: I don't mean forcing everything to sound positive, though. Grief is grief, and danger should be called danger. Harm and anger still need accurate words, and so do limits and accountability. Consent too, and whatever practical constraints there are. Some of those are hard to say to someone you're comforting. Once what's real has been named, spend most of your energy on what can be protected, practiced, repaired, chosen or grown. If nobody needs a picture of what the person shouldn't become, leave it out.
t65z13_st1p3w2p1: Before you advise your little one, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: "Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, give you ideas, or some mix?" Same goes for anybody else. You don't have to ask every time, like a ritual. When it's obvious which they want, follow that. If you'd only be guessing, though, one sentence can keep you from giving advice to somebody who needed to be heard. Or from just listening when they wanted help thinking it through.
t65z13_st1p5w2p1: This can be the healthiest way to borrow adulthood. Your peer doesn't become your permanent parent, though your little one might wish they would. They show you a bit of adulting and help you join in. At some point they hand it back to you. Therapy stays useful for what therapy does. Community and disciplined peer support like this do something different, and a serious healing path can include both.
t65z13_st1p6w2p1: Community can work in both directions. Sometimes loving people help you feel safe and like you belong, enough that a deeper opening becomes possible. Your little one might be checking whether they mean it. Other times the opening comes first and changes what kinds of people and relationships you can "manifest." Then community helps make the opening practical and real, something your body knows. The door you came in through matters less than the loop. Love moves from spiritual experience to your little one, then into the grown-up relationship. From you it goes into other people, and back again.

t65z13_secfg1all8:
# How to Forgive Without Forgetting

Maybe someone's told you that you'll never heal until you forgive. For a lot of people, healing does eventually include some forgiveness, or at least getting out from under active resentment. But it can't be put on a schedule, and you don't need it first to be safe, set a boundary or hold anyone accountable. Justice and recovering don't wait on it either. Resentment does narrow what you can see, though, and it keeps your little one organized around the injury. Forcing forgiveness early just gets you an enlightened-looking act while the wound goes underground.

What can help is seeing how they got there. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn't handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you've held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

None of that makes what they did harmless, and it doesn't mean nothing else was possible in theory. It means punishing them can't reach back and hand them the awareness or support they didn't have. You might still wish it could. The useful part is repairing what can be repaired, and making a different response easier from here on. The harm is real, and accountability stays. Boundaries can still be right, and so can legal consequences, moral judgment or staying away for good. Understanding them doesn't cancel any of that, and neither does forgiving them. "I understand how you became this way" can sit right next to "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."

Forgiving yourself works the same way, and if that's hard, forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Own what you did, and only what was yours. Let the remorse land ("oh no, I really did that"). Repair what you can, with an apology or amends, or by changing what you do. After that you're allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and that might feel like getting away with something. The responsibility stays, though. Some harms take years. Forgiving too soon is one trap, and living inside resentment for good is the other. So don't push it. Keep coming back to how they became capable of it, until the understanding is real enough to change how you feel.
